_comment: Cambridge 0097's Thinking and Working Scientifically and Science in Context objectives for Stage 1 that no Grade 1 unit reached, authored as reasoning prompts. Added 2026-09-17 with the Stages 1-4 re-point: the shell course had been measured against the 2018 framework, which has far fewer of these, and 0097 asks for four TWS strands plus Science in Context from Stage 1 onwards. Every prompt is anchored to an investigation Grade 1 already runs. The register is a six-year-old's: one question, a concrete object they have handled, and a model answer of one or two sentences. TWS and SIC are not topics - they are how an investigation the unit ALREADY does is framed - so nothing new is being taught here, it is being asked for.
_vehicle: reasoningPrompts. The builder appends these to the named unit's own array. At Stages 1-4 the section is deck-only, and shell/subjects/science.js :: renderExplainThinkingDeck renders one prompt per slide with the prompt, a textarea, the key ideas behind a disclosure and the model answer behind another. Checked before choosing it at these stages: the deck maps prompts to slides one for one, so appending adds slides rather than renumbering them; completion is stored by item id in progress.reasoning, so authored ids keep their own identity; and complete() in course-app.js is add-only, so a learner who finished four of four keeps the tick and meets the new prompts as further work.
source: Authored 2026-09-17 against Cambridge 0097 Stage 1, anchored to the investigations in Grade 1 units 1-6. Not extracted from a book: the Teacher's Resource frames these for a teacher to deliver aloud, and this course has no teacher in the room.
_minimumCovered: One prompt per unclaimed Stage 1 TWS/SIC objective, plus two added 2026-09-18 for objectives that were cited but never actually asked of a learner (1SIC.04, 1TWSc.04 - see their own prompts for what was missing). Coverage is a number that only goes up.

prompts.prompt: A goat is sick. Who in your town knows how to help it get better, and how did they learn?
keyIdeas: A vet is a doctor for animals
A farmer knows about animals too
They learned by looking carefully, like a scientist
prompts.modelAnswer: A vet is an animal doctor, and a farmer who keeps goats knows a lot too. They learned by watching animals carefully for a long time and finding out what makes them well again. That is science, and it is their job.

prompts.prompt: You are growing a bean in a jar. Why must you use the jar and not a bowl with no sides, and why do you pour the water in slowly?
keyIdeas: The jar holds the bean and the water together
You can see through the jar
Slow pouring does not wash the bean away
prompts.modelAnswer: The jar keeps the bean and the water in one place and you can see through the side to watch the root grow. Pouring slowly means the water does not push the bean out of its place. Using the right thing, the right way, is part of doing science well.

prompts.prompt: Your bean shoot has grown. You have no ruler. How could you measure how tall it is using your hand or some paper clips?
keyIdeas: Count how many paper clips tall it is
Count finger widths, always the same finger
Write the number in your plant diary
prompts.modelAnswer: I can lay paper clips end to end beside the shoot and count them, or count how many of my finger widths tall it is. I must use the same finger or the same paper clips every day, or the numbers will not match. Then I write the number in my plant diary.

prompts.prompt: Long ago, people did not know that washing your hands keeps you well. What do we know now that they did not?
keyIdeas: Long ago people did not know about germs
Germs are too small to see
Now we know washing hands takes germs away
prompts.modelAnswer: Long ago nobody knew that tiny germs, too small to see, can make you ill. Now we know, so we wash our hands with soap before we eat. People learned this by looking very carefully, and what we know changed.

prompts.prompt: A drum makes a sound when you hit it. Use what you learned about shaking to explain why.
keyIdeas: The drum skin shakes when you hit it
Shaking makes the sound
When the shaking stops, the sound stops
prompts.modelAnswer: When you hit the drum, the skin on top shakes very fast, and that shaking makes the sound you hear. If you hold the skin with your hand it cannot shake, so the sound stops. Science explains how the drum in your house works.

prompts.prompt: You know a goat needs water every day to stay alive. If nobody gave it water for many days, what would happen - and whose doing would that be?
keyIdeas: Without water the goat would get weak and could die
That happens because of what a person did or did not do
Knowing what living things need helps us look after them
prompts.modelAnswer: If nobody gave the goat water, it would get weaker and weaker, because water is one of the things it needs to stay alive. That would not just happen by itself - it would happen because of what a person did or did not do. Knowing what a living thing needs is what lets us look after it, instead of hurting it without meaning to.

prompts.prompt: Before you shake a tin full of stones to make a sound, name one thing you should check first to do it safely.
keyIdeas: Ask an adult before using something you find at home
Check the tin has no sharp or broken edges
Hold it away from your face while you shake it
prompts.modelAnswer: Before I shake the tin, I ask an adult if I may use it, and I check that the edges are not sharp or broken. I hold it away from my face while I shake it, in case anything falls out. Checking that first is following instructions safely, not just starting straight away.
